chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Durust, from Zurara, from one of the two of them (peace be upon them both) who said:
Staying awake at night due to illness or pain is superior and greater in reward than a year of worship.

key_terms.أَجْر: Reward/recompense from God for deeds or endurance
key_terms.سَهَر: Staying awake/sleeplessness at night — used here for involuntary wakefulness caused by illness
key_terms.عِبَادَة: Worship — encompasses all devotional acts including prayer, fasting, and supplication

ai.seo_question: Is staying awake due to illness considered worship in Islam?
ai.summary: The Imam (either al-Baqir or al-Sadiq, peace be upon them) teaches that the involuntary suffering of a sick person who is kept awake through illness or pain carries a reward that surpasses an entire year of voluntary worship. This hadith reflects a core principle in Shia ethics: that patient endurance of hardship and suffering — especially when borne with faith — is itself a form of worship that God values immensely. For early Muslim communities, this teaching offered profound consolation to the sick and those caring for them.
word_analysis: one of the two of them
